lead: In an ideal gas mixture the molecules ignore each other: no attraction, no reaction, and each gas fills the whole vessel at the mixture temperature. Dalton splits the total pressure into partial pressures p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p; Amagat splits the total volume into partial volumes V<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>V. Both use the mole fraction y<sub>i</sub> as the share. Engineers need this for air, combustion products, LPG–air and natural gas lines, where a compressor or a pipe must be sized for the mixture, not for one gas.
prereq: You need: the ideal gas law pV = nRuT and the kmol from 5.7 Ideal and real gases, plus pressure and the mole concept from the basic concepts.

sections.h3: Mole fraction and mixture molar mass

blocks.text: An ideal gas mixture is a set of gases sharing one vessel at the same temperature T and pressure p, with no chemical reaction and no forces between molecules. Amounts are in kilomoles: one kmol of gas i has mass M<sub>i</sub> kg, and the total is n = n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub> + ….

The mole fraction of component i is y<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n. It is dimensionless, and Σ y<sub>i</sub> = 1. The mass fraction w<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>i</sub>/m is a different number; for air, y<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.21 but w<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.23. The two are linked by w<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub>/M<sub>mix</sub>.

A mixture behaves as one gas with molar mass M<sub>mix</sub> = m/n = Σ y<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub> and gas constant R<sub>mix</sub> = R<sub>u</sub>/M<sub>mix</sub>, where R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K) is the universal gas constant.

y<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n is the mole fraction, dimensionless; M<sub>i</sub> is the molar mass of component i in kg/kmol; M<sub>mix</sub> is the mixture molar mass in kg/kmol; R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K); R<sub>mix</sub> is the mixture gas constant in kJ/(kg·K).

Dalton's model takes the mixture apart. Put component i alone in the same volume V at the same temperature T. It behaves as an ideal gas and presses on the walls with the partial pressure p<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T/V. Dalton's law states that the mixture pressure is the sum of these partial pressures: p = Σ p<sub>i</sub>.

Divide p<sub>i</sub> by p = nR<sub>u</sub>T/V and the temperature and volume cancel: p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p. The partial pressure is a share of the total, and the share is the mole fraction. Using the mass fraction here is the most common error in this chapter.

The V and T in p = nR<sub>u</sub>T/V belong to the whole mixture, with R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K) giving p in kPa. In the example below, oxygen and nitrogen share one 2 m³ tank; nitrogen is not squeezed into a smaller volume of its own.

Amagat's model keeps the mixture pressure p and temperature T and asks a different question: what volume V<sub>i</sub> would component i occupy alone at p and T? For an ideal gas, V<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T/p = y<sub>i</sub>V. Amagat's law states that the partial volumes add to the vessel volume: V = Σ V<sub>i</sub>.

The same mole fraction appears in both laws: p<sub>i</sub>/p = V<sub>i</sub>/V = y<sub>i</sub>. Dalton and Amagat are two ways of bookkeeping the same ideal-gas model, not two different physical pictures. Use Dalton when a pressure gauge is read. Use Amagat when a gas analyser reports percentages by volume, because for ideal gases volume per cent equals mole per cent.

Mixture properties follow the Gibbs–Dalton rule: u<sub>mix</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>u<sub>i</sub> and h<sub>mix</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub> per kmol, each component property taken at the mixture temperature; per kg the weights are the mass fractions, c<sub>p,mix</sub> = Σ w<sub>i</sub>c<sub>p,i</sub>. Mixing is irreversible, so entropy rises even when T and p do not change. For ideal gases that start separate at the same T and p, ΔS = −R<sub>u</sub> Σ n<sub>i</sub> ln y<sub>i</sub>, which is positive because every y<sub>i</sub> < 1.

Some old notes write Amalgam's law for Amagat's law; the correct name is Amagat. Both laws assume ideal gases. At 200 bar, or near condensation, they fail, and a real mixture needs the compressibility factor of 5.8. Kay's rule gives the pseudocritical values to enter the chart with: T′c = Σ yiTc,i and p′c = Σ yipc,i.

examples.question: A rigid tank of 2 m³ holds 0.8 kg of oxygen and 2.8 kg of nitrogen at 300 K. Take R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K), M<sub>O2</sub> = 32 kg/kmol and M<sub>N2</sub> = 28 kg/kmol. Find the mole fractions, the total and partial pressures, the partial volumes, the mixture molar mass and gas constant, and the entropy generated if the two gases were first held apart at the same T and p and then allowed to mix.
steps: Moles: n<sub>O2</sub> = 0.8/32 = 0.025 kmol and n<sub>N2</sub> = 2.8/28 = 0.100 kmol, so n = 0.125 kmol.
Mole fractions: y<sub>O2</sub> = 0.025/0.125 = 0.2 and y<sub>N2</sub> = 0.100/0.125 = 0.8; check 0.2 + 0.8 = 1.00. (Mass fractions are different: w<sub>O2</sub> = 0.8/3.6 = 0.222.)
Amagat: V<sub>O2</sub> = 0.2 × 2 = 0.4 m³ and V<sub>N2</sub> = 0.8 × 2 = 1.6 m³; together 2 m³.
Check: pV/m = 155.9 × 2/3.6 = 86.6 kJ/kg and R<sub>mix</sub>T = 0.2887 × 300 = 86.6 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: y<sub>O2</sub> = 0.2, y<sub>N2</sub> = 0.8; p = 155.9 kPa with p<sub>O2</sub> = 31.2 kPa and p<sub>N2</sub> = 124.7 kPa; V<sub>O2</sub> = 0.4 m³, V<sub>N2</sub> = 1.6 m³; M<sub>mix</sub> = 28.8 kg/kmol, R<sub>mix</sub> = 0.2887 kJ/(kg·K); ΔS of mixing = 0.520 kJ/K.

traps: p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p, never p<sub>i</sub> = w<sub>i</sub>p. Air is 0.21 oxygen by mole but 0.23 by mass, so the mass fraction overstates p<sub>O2</sub> by about 10 %.
Partial pressure uses the mixture volume V and the mixture temperature T. Putting a component's own volume into p<sub>i</sub>V = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T is the classic mistake.
Mixing unit sets. R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 works with kPa, m³ and kmol, or with Pa, m³ and mol. Putting MPa with m³, or mol with kmol, shifts the answer by a factor of 1000.
The mole fractions must add to 1.00. If an analysis sums to 0.95, a component is missing, not a rounding error.
Amagat's partial volume is not the volume of the gas before mixing. It is the volume that gas would occupy alone at the final p and T.

quiz.q: State Dalton's law of partial pressures and write the formula for the partial pressure of component i.
quiz.a: The total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures, p = Σ p<sub>i</sub>. Each gas alone in the mixture volume V at temperature T gives p<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T/V = y<sub>i</sub>p.

quiz.q: Why do Dalton's and Amagat's laws give the same mole fractions for an ideal gas mixture?
quiz.a: For an ideal gas pV = nR<sub>u</sub>T holds for the whole mixture and for each component at the same T. So p<sub>i</sub>/p = n<sub>i</sub>/n = V<sub>i</sub>/V = y<sub>i</sub>; the two laws are the same equation rearranged.

quiz.q: A 2 m³ tank at 400 K holds 0.05 kmol of CO₂ and 0.15 kmol of N₂. Take R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K). Find the total pressure and the partial pressure of CO₂.
A 4 kg mixture contains 1 kg of O₂ (M = 32 kg/kmol) and 3 kg of N₂ (M = 28 kg/kmol). Find the mole fractions and the mixture molar mass.
A student reports p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.23 bar in air at 1 bar, because oxygen is 23 % by mass. Identify the error and give the correct partial pressure.
quiz.a: 0.23 is a mass fraction. Dalton's law needs the mole fraction y<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21, so p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21 × 1 bar = 0.21 bar. A mass fraction cannot be substituted into p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p.

quiz.q: Why does entropy rise when two ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure mix, though no heat is added?
quiz.a: Mixing is irreversible: the gases never unmix by themselves. Each gas expands from its own partial volume into the whole vessel, so ΔS = −R<sub>u</sub> Σ n<sub>i</sub> ln y<sub>i</sub> > 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real gas mixtures at high pressure are handled with cubic equations of state plus mixing rules, and in chemical engineering through the fugacity of each component. Search next for pseudo-critical properties and the fugacity coefficient.
